title: Ecosystems
description: An ecosystem is a community of living things and their environment. Food chains and webs show how energy moves from plants to animals. Every organism has a role.

exercises.question: What is an ECOSYSTEM?
choices: only the animals in an area
all the living and non-living things in an area and how they interact
only the plants in a forest
the weather in a region
exercises.exp: An ecosystem includes ALL living things (plants, animals, fungi) AND non-living things (water, air, soil) in an area.

exercises.question: In a food chain, energy comes ORIGINALLY from ___.
choices: animals eating other animals
the sun
the soil
rain
exercises.exp: The sun is the original source of energy in nearly all food chains — plants capture it through photosynthesis.

exercises.question: In a food chain: Grass → Rabbit → Fox. What role does the GRASS play?
choices: consumer
predator
producer
decomposer
exercises.exp: Grass is a producer — it makes its own food using sunlight and is the base of the food chain.

exercises.question: In a food chain: Grass → Rabbit → Fox. What role does the RABBIT play?
choices: producer
primary consumer
apex predator
decomposer
exercises.exp: The rabbit eats plants — it is a primary (first-level) consumer.

exercises.question: What is a DECOMPOSER?
choices: an animal that only eats plants
an organism that breaks down dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil
an animal at the top of the food chain
a plant that catches insects
exercises.exp: Decomposers like fungi and bacteria break down dead organisms, recycling nutrients back into the soil.

exercises.question: A FOOD WEB is ___.
choices: a single chain of what eats what
many interconnected food chains showing feeding relationships
a spider's web used to catch food
a diagram of only plant growth
exercises.exp: A food web shows many overlapping food chains — most animals eat more than one type of food!

exercises.question: What happens to a forest ecosystem if all the WOLVES are removed?
choices: the deer population stays the same
the deer population grows, overgrazing and harming plant life
plants grow more with fewer animals
nothing changes
exercises.exp: Without wolves (predators), deer numbers explode and eat too many plants — the whole ecosystem is affected!

exercises.question: Which of these best describes a PREDATOR?
choices: an animal that is hunted for food
an animal that hunts other animals for food
a plant that makes food
an organism that eats dead matter
exercises.exp: A predator hunts and eats other animals (prey). A wolf is a predator; a rabbit is prey.

exercises.question: What does MATTER do in a food chain?
choices: it disappears when eaten
it is created by animals
it moves from one organism to the next as they eat each other
it only stays in plants
exercises.exp: Matter (like carbon and nitrogen) moves through a food chain — from plants to herbivores to carnivores to decomposers.

exercises.question: Which ecosystem is described: 'hot and dry, little rainfall, cactus and lizards live here'?
choices: rainforest
arctic tundra
desert
ocean
exercises.exp: Deserts are hot and dry with little rain. Cacti store water, and lizards are adapted to the heat.

exercises.question: What role do BEES play in ecosystems?
choices: they are decomposers
they are pollinators that help plants reproduce
they are apex predators
they produce oxygen directly
exercises.exp: Bees carry pollen between flowers, helping plants reproduce — they are essential pollinators!

exercises.question: In a healthy ecosystem, which is true?
choices: only one species survives
producers, consumers, and decomposers are all present and balanced
predators always outnumber prey
plants do not need animals
exercises.exp: A healthy ecosystem has balance — producers make food, consumers eat it, and decomposers recycle nutrients.

exercises.question: What is a HABITAT?
choices: the food an animal eats
the natural environment where an organism lives and finds everything it needs to survive
the number of animals in an area
the weather of a region
exercises.exp: A habitat is an organism's natural home — providing food, water, shelter, and space. Polar bears live in Arctic habitats; frogs in wetland habitats.

exercises.question: What is a NICHE?
choices: a small cave where animals sleep
an organism's role in its ecosystem — what it eats, what eats it, and how it interacts with its environment
the number of organisms in a population
an organism's physical appearance
exercises.exp: A niche is an organism's complete role — what it eats, when it is active, where it lives, what eats it. No two species can occupy exactly the same niche!

exercises.question: ENERGY in a food chain is lost at each level. What happens to it?
choices: it is destroyed and disappears
energy is converted to heat and used for life functions — only about 10% passes to the next level
all energy is perfectly transferred
energy increases at each level
exercises.exp: At each level, about 90% of energy is used for life processes (movement, warmth, growth) and lost as heat — only ~10% transfers up the chain!

exercises.question: Because of energy loss in food chains, there are usually FEWER ___.
choices: producers than herbivores
predators than prey at the top of a food chain
herbivores than plants
plants than bacteria
exercises.exp: Energy is lost at each level — so each level can support fewer organisms. More plants than herbivores, more herbivores than carnivores. This forms a pyramid!

exercises.question: SYMBIOSIS describes ___.
choices: two organisms competing to the death
a close, long-term relationship between two different species
organisms living in different ecosystems
animals eating the same food
exercises.exp: Symbiosis is any close, long-term interaction between species — it includes mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism.

exercises.question: A TICK on a dog feeds on the dog's blood. The tick benefits; the dog is harmed. This is ___.
choices: mutualism
commensalism
parasitism
predation
exercises.exp: Parasitism: the parasite (tick) benefits; the host (dog) is harmed but not killed (usually). Differs from predation where the host is killed.

exercises.question: What role do FUNGI play in ecosystems?
choices: they are producers like plants
they are primary consumers
they are decomposers — breaking down dead organic matter into nutrients
they are apex predators
exercises.exp: Fungi are key decomposers — their enzymes break down dead wood, leaves, and animals, releasing nutrients back into the soil for plants to use. No fungi = no nutrient cycling!

exercises.question: If a disease wiped out ALL the RABBITS in a meadow ecosystem, what would most likely happen to the FOX population?
choices: foxes would grow larger
fox population would increase with no competition
fox population would decline — losing a major food source
foxes would switch to only eating grass
exercises.exp: Less prey = less food for predators. Fox numbers would fall. This shows how interconnected species are — one change ripples through the whole food web!

exercises.question: What is CARRYING CAPACITY?
choices: the maximum weight a bridge can hold
the maximum population size an ecosystem can support given available resources
the minimum number of animals for a healthy population
the amount of food each animal needs daily
exercises.exp: Carrying capacity: the maximum population size an ecosystem's resources (food, water, space, shelter) can sustainably support. Exceed it and the population crashes!

exercises.question: INVASIVE SPECIES are non-native species introduced to a new ecosystem. Why are they often harmful?
choices: they make ecosystems more biodiverse always
they lack natural predators in the new ecosystem and can outcompete native species, disrupting the food web
they always help native animals find food
invasive species always die out quickly
exercises.exp: Without natural predators to control them, invasive species can multiply explosively — outcompeting natives for food and space. Zebra mussels, kudzu, and European starlings are examples.

exercises.question: What is a BIOTIC factor in an ecosystem?
choices: temperature and rainfall
any living component — plants, animals, fungi, bacteria
soil type and sunlight
wind speed and direction
exercises.exp: Biotic factors are the living parts of an ecosystem — all organisms. Abiotic factors are non-living (temperature, water, sunlight, soil).

exercises.question: What is an ABIOTIC factor in an ecosystem?
choices: a predator
a tree
the amount of sunlight reaching the forest floor
a decomposer
exercises.exp: Abiotic factors are non-living physical and chemical factors — sunlight, temperature, water, soil type, wind. They shape which organisms can live in an area.

exercises.question: OCEAN PHYTOPLANKTON (tiny photosynthetic organisms) produce about HALF of Earth's oxygen. What would happen if they disappeared?
choices: nothing — they are too small to matter
oxygen levels in the atmosphere would crash, threatening most life on Earth
fish populations would only slightly decrease
land plants would produce double the oxygen
exercises.exp: Phytoplankton are the base of ocean food chains AND produce ~50% of atmospheric oxygen. Their loss would devastate both ocean ecosystems and Earth's oxygen supply.

exercises.question: A FOOD PYRAMID shows less energy at the TOP. Why are there few APEX PREDATORS?
choices: apex predators are lazy
so little energy reaches the top of the food chain that it can only support a few large predators
predators choose to stay rare
apex predators require very little energy
exercises.exp: Each trophic level loses ~90% of energy — by the time energy reaches apex predators, so little remains that only a few individuals can be supported.

exercises.question: DEFORESTATION (cutting down forests) affects ecosystems because ___.
choices: more sunlight makes other plants grow faster
habitat is destroyed, disrupting food webs, reducing biodiversity, and releasing stored carbon
fewer trees means less competition for animals
deforestation only affects the trees
exercises.exp: Forests are complex ecosystems — remove the trees and species lose habitat, food webs collapse, soil erodes, water cycles change, and huge amounts of stored carbon release into the atmosphere.

exercises.question: The WATER CYCLE connects ecosystems by ___.
choices: keeping all water in one location
moving water between land, ocean, and atmosphere — connecting distant ecosystems through shared water
only affecting ocean ecosystems
blocking water from reaching land ecosystems
exercises.exp: Water evaporates from oceans, falls as rain on forests, runs into rivers, and flows back to the sea — the water cycle links all Earth's ecosystems.

exercises.question: COMPETITION in ecosystems occurs when ___.
choices: two organisms cooperate to find food
two or more organisms need the same limited resource (food, space, water, mates) at the same time
predators hunt prey
decomposers break down dead matter
exercises.exp: Competition: organisms fight for the same limited resources. Two robin species competing for the same insects is interspecific competition; two robins competing is intraspecific.

exercises.question: WOLVES were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995. This caused trees to REGROW along riverbanks. How?
choices: wolves planted trees
wolves chased elk away from riverbanks — allowing riverside trees (which elk had overgrazen) to regrow, stabilising riverbanks
wolves brought seeds from other parks
wolves dug irrigation channels
exercises.exp: A trophic cascade! Wolves hunted elk → elk avoided river valleys → riverside vegetation regrew → rivers became more stable. Predators shape entire ecosystems!

exercises.question: An ecosystem with HIGH BIODIVERSITY is generally ___.
choices: less stable — too many species cause chaos
more stable and resilient — if one species is lost, others can fill its role
identical to a low-diversity ecosystem
harder for all species to survive
exercises.exp: High biodiversity = more redundancy. If one pollinator disappears, others remain. More complex food webs are more resistant to disturbance — biodiversity is insurance!

exercises.question: CARBON cycles through ecosystems. Plants absorb CO₂ for photosynthesis; animals release CO₂ through respiration. Decomposers release CO₂ when breaking down dead matter. This shows ___.
choices: carbon is destroyed in ecosystems
matter is cycled through ecosystems continuously — the same carbon atoms pass through many organisms over time
carbon only flows one way through ecosystems
carbon is only stored in animals
exercises.exp: The carbon cycle: CO₂ → plants (photosynthesis) → animals (eating) → decomposers (breaking down) → CO₂ again. The same carbon atoms cycle endlessly through life!

exercises.question: What is an ECOSYSTEM?
choices: only the plants in an area
only the animals in an area
all the living organisms AND non-living things (soil, water, air, sunlight) in an area, interacting as a system
only the largest animals in a habitat
exercises.exp: An ecosystem includes ALL living things (biotic) AND non-living components (abiotic) — soil, water, air, temperature, light. Everything interacts!

exercises.question: PRODUCERS are always at the BASE of food webs because ___.
choices: they are the largest organisms
they capture energy from sunlight (photosynthesis) and convert it into organic matter that all other life depends on
they are the most numerous animals
they consume the most energy
exercises.exp: Producers (plants, algae) convert solar energy to chemical energy (food). All energy in the food web ultimately comes from producers. No producers = no life!

exercises.question: Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. Where does the other 90% go?
choices: it is recycled back to producers
it is stored in the soil
it is lost as heat through respiration and other metabolic processes
it moves to decomposers only
exercises.exp: The 10% rule: only ~10% of energy transfers to the next level. The other 90% is lost as heat (respiration, movement, maintaining body temperature). That is why food chains are short!

exercises.question: The NITROGEN CYCLE involves bacteria converting ___.
choices: oxygen into nitrogen in the air
nitrogen gas (N₂) from the air into ammonium and nitrates that plants can use; then back to N₂
carbon into nitrogen
water into nitrogen compounds
exercises.exp: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert N₂ → ammonium. Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium → nitrates (plant food). Denitrifying bacteria return nitrates → N₂. The cycle continues!

exercises.question: INVASIVE SPECIES cause problems in ecosystems because ___.
choices: they are always bigger than native species
they have no natural predators in the new environment, so their populations grow unchecked and they outcompete native species
they are always poisonous
they eat only plants and never animals
exercises.exp: Without natural predators or diseases to control them, invasive species outcompete natives for food and habitat. They can devastate ecosystems. Example: cane toads in Australia!

exercises.question: HABITAT DESTRUCTION is the biggest cause of species loss. Which human activity causes the MOST habitat destruction globally?
choices: sport fishing
converting forests to agricultural land (deforestation)
building roads only
tourism in national parks
exercises.exp: Agricultural expansion destroys more habitat than any other activity — especially tropical deforestation. About 50% of Earth's forests have been cleared in the last 10,000 years.

exercises.question: The WATER CYCLE provides fresh water to ecosystems. Which step directly fills rivers and groundwater?
choices: evaporation
transpiration
precipitation (rain/snow falling) and runoff
condensation forming clouds
exercises.exp: Precipitation falls as rain or snow. It runs off into rivers, seeps into soil (groundwater), or feeds lakes — replenishing freshwater that all land ecosystems depend on!

exercises.question: DEFORESTATION increases CO₂ in the atmosphere because ___.
choices: trees release CO₂ as they grow
cutting trees releases stored carbon AND removes the trees that were absorbing CO₂ — double impact
forests produce methane, not CO₂
trees only absorb CO₂ when they flower
exercises.exp: Double whammy: cut trees release stored carbon + no more photosynthesis to remove new CO₂. Forests are carbon sinks — losing them accelerates climate change!

exercises.question: What is a FOOD WEB?
choices: the digestive system of an animal
a single sequence of who eats whom
a complex network of interconnected food chains showing all feeding relationships in an ecosystem
only the plant-animal feeding relationships
exercises.exp: Food webs show the complex, interconnected feeding relationships in an ecosystem. Most animals eat and are eaten by multiple species — webs, not simple chains!

exercises.question: DECOMPOSERS are critical to ecosystems because ___.
choices: they are at the top of the food chain
they compete with all other organisms for food
they break down dead organic matter, releasing nutrients back into the soil for producers to use again
they produce oxygen through photosynthesis
exercises.exp: Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up and nutrients would be locked away. Decomposers recycle nutrients — feeding the plants that feed everything else!

exercises.question: CLIMATE CHANGE affects ecosystems by ___.
choices: only increasing rainfall
only affecting ocean temperatures
shifting seasons, altering precipitation, and warming temperatures — changing which species can survive where, disrupting migration and breeding
making deserts wetter and forests drier uniformly
exercises.exp: Climate change alters temperature and precipitation patterns — species cannot adapt fast enough. Coral bleaching, Arctic ice loss, and shifting seasons all impact ecosystems!

exercises.question: In the OCEAN, phytoplankton are the primary producers. If phytoplankton populations CRASHED, what would happen?
choices: only fish near the surface would be affected
the whole ocean food web would collapse — all consumers that depend on phytoplankton (directly or indirectly) would lose their food source
krill and small fish would still survive
only warm-water species would be affected
exercises.exp: Phytoplankton produce about half of Earth's oxygen AND form the base of the entire ocean food web. Their loss would cascade through ALL marine life!

exercises.question: What is the GREENHOUSE EFFECT?
choices: how greenhouses trap heat for plants
the process where greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, water vapour) in the atmosphere trap infrared radiation from Earth's surface, warming the planet
a completely harmful process that should be eliminated
something only affecting tropical regions
exercises.exp: The greenhouse effect is natural and essential — without it, Earth would be -18°C. The problem is ENHANCED greenhouse effect: too much CO₂ traps too much heat!

exercises.question: BIODIVERSITY HOTSPOTS are areas with ___.
choices: the most volcanoes
the highest number of endemic species AND serious threats to those species
the most rainfall on Earth
the largest land area
exercises.exp: Hotspots: areas with extraordinary species richness (many endemic species found nowhere else) AND major habitat loss threats. Tropical forests and islands are typical hotspots.

exercises.question: Which human action would MOST help restore a degraded ecosystem?
choices: introducing more non-native predators
replanting native vegetation and removing invasive species to restore the original food web structure
adding artificial fertilisers to all soils
building more roads through the ecosystem
exercises.exp: Restoring native plants reestablishes habitat, which attracts native animals. Removing invasives reduces competition. This combination rebuilds the original ecosystem structure!

exercises.question: What is EUTROPHICATION of water bodies?
choices: water becoming too cold for life
the over-enrichment of water with nutrients (especially nitrates from fertilisers) causing algal blooms that deplete oxygen, killing aquatic life
water becoming too pure and lacking minerals
water freezing during eutrophication events
exercises.exp: Fertiliser runoff → algal bloom → algae die → decomposers respire → oxygen depleted (hypoxia) → fish and invertebrates die. A major water pollution problem worldwide!

exercises.question: PROTECTED AREAS (national parks, marine reserves) help biodiversity by ___.
choices: eliminating all human activity which harms wildlife
providing safe habitats where species can live and reproduce without hunting, habitat destruction, or pollution pressure
preventing all scientific research on wild species
guaranteeing no species ever goes extinct within their boundaries
exercises.exp: Protected areas reduce the main threats: habitat loss, hunting, and pollution. Species populations in well-managed reserves often recover. They act as refuges and gene banks!

exercises.question: The PHOSPHORUS CYCLE differs from carbon and nitrogen cycles because ___.
choices: phosphorus does not cycle at all
phosphorus has no atmospheric component — it moves through rocks, soil, water, and organisms without a gas phase
phosphorus only cycles in oceans
phosphorus is cycled only by bacteria
exercises.exp: Unlike carbon (CO₂ in air) and nitrogen (N₂ in air), phosphorus has no gaseous phase. It weathers from rocks → soil → plants → animals → decomposers → soil. Slow geological cycle!
